newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ford turns to Mexican plant to boost sales.
newsitem.headline: Ford turns to Mexican plant to boost sales.

text.p: As it has in the past, Ford Motor Co is turning once again to its landmark plant in the northern Mexican desert to boost flagging sales and give the carmaker a new image, analysts said.

The 1998 Ford Escort ZX2 Coupe, a sportier version of past Escort models, will be built exclusively in Hermosillo, about 165 miles (265 km) south of the Arizona border. The company was to officially launch the new model on Wednesday.

"They're kind of following a trend in the industry which is, one, to appear to the customer to be a fun company with a sporty car but, two, not to spend too much money doing it," Lincoln Merrihew, an analyst with DRI/McGraw-Hill in Lexington, Mass., told Reuters. "The Escort Coupe kind of satisfies both objectives."
This is the same assembly plant that came as such a surprise to the automotive world after it came on line in 1986.
Though the Big Three had been building cars in Mexico for the local market for decades, this was the first plant started up specifically for exporting to the U.S. market.

Ford chose to make here its Ford Escort and nearly identical Mercury Tracer models, high-volume sellers key to grabbing a share of the small-car market at a time when the Big Three were still trying to overcome their image of making nothing but gas-guzzlers.

But after the Escort became one of the top-selling cars in the United States in the 1980s, becoming the No. 1 passenger car one year, it slumped to No. 11 overall in 1996 with sales of 284,644 units, down from 285,570 in 1995, trailing the Honda Civic/Del Sol (286,350 in 1996) while the Chevrolet Cavalier (277,222 in 1996, up from 212,767 in 1995) gained ground.

"Maintaining that level of being among the top sellers makes you put out more effort because at the same time there are a lot eyes watching, more customers to satisfy," Plant Manager Jose Islas told Reuters. "It showed that a Mexican plant could go out and compete in the international markets."
The new Coupe has yet to hit the market, so it remains to be seen whether the new design will muster up greater sales.

During a recent tour of the plant by Reuters, Ford workers appeared to be enjoying the ride, zipping out of the factory in the brand new test models, tires screaching as they lined up shiny new Coupes in a row.
Ford wouldn't allow a Reuters photographer to take the redesigned Escort's picture, lest the competition get a premature look before the official unveiling on Wednesday.

"The Escort is in need of a makeover," said George Magliano of the WEFA Group in New York."It's gotten old and they're coming out with a redesigned, sportier version. They need to jazz up sales because it's been around a while and is suffering at the hands of the competition."
Islas, the plant manager, said his team was up to the job.

Aside from being the pride of Hermosillo, a city of 900,000 whose economy in the past relied on agriculture and mining, the plant here has been a major success story for Ford, turning out 40 units per hour over two shifts, almost entirely for the U.S. and Canadian markets, Islas said.
Hermosillo makes the Coupe and the Escort station wagon while Ford's plant in Wayne, Mich., makes the four-door Escort as well as the wagon on two shifts, producing 74 units per hour.
When Ford opened shop in Hermosillo, it created a new system of quality control by making each manager responsible for his area and allowing workers to solve problems directly.
"Really, we have been breaking the mold," Islas said.
Islas noted some small details, such as how he and others in management wear the same uniform as production line workers and how they all eat the same food in the same cafeteria.

When Islas went to pour his own coffee in a disposable cup, he passed through a conference room where workers were holding a meeting. The workers joked and bantered with Islas instead of breaking into silence when the boss entered the room.
The neatly groomed and educated workers, filing in to work on time, are are far cry from the old stereotype of a sombero-wearing Mexican sleeping under a cactus tree.

"Here we have demonstrated that we have the best quality within the industry," Islas said. "I'm not talking about Ford Motor Company but rather the industry in general. I can compare this plant with any other in the world."
